To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the water import into tomato fruit is reduced by high soil salinity and is conducted by both xylem and phloem, and that the osmotic potential of mature fruit is dominated by potassium salts.
the water and potassium salts accumulated in the fruit are imported from the phloem, and that the contribution of the xylem water to total water accumulation is small.
the osmotic concentration of tomato fruit was determined by potassium and hexose salts and that potassium salts were the dominant osmotic solutes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accumulation of water in the fruit, and its contribution to fruit growth.
the accumulation of water, dry matter, potassium, hexoses, calcium, and osmotic potential in tomato fruit.
the accumulation of dry matter and the regulation of osmotic potential in tomato fruit grown at different levels of salinity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the accumulation of dry matter in tomato fruits is determined by the rate of phloem water transport, which in turn is determined by the water status and the rate of transpiration.
tomato fruits grown at high salinity have a lower rate of water import, but a similar rate of dry matter accumulation, to fruits grown at low salinity.
tomato fruit growth is controlled primarily by the phloem supply of water and dry mass and the phloem water supply is in turn regulated by the transpiration rate of the leaves.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the accumulation of dry matter in the fruit was not influenced by the salinity of the nutrient solutions.

the accumulation of potassium salts in tomato fruit is a major factor in determining the osmotic potential of fruit, and that the concentration of these in the phloem stream decreases during fruit development.

the accumulation of water in tomato fruit was controlled by the rate of phloem import, and that the osmotic potential of young tomato fruit was regulated by potassium salts and hexoses, with the contribution of the two components being dependent on the salinity of the growing medium.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the accumulation of dry matter and the concentration of potassium in the fruit of tomatoes grown at different salinity are regulated in such a way as to keep the osmotic potential of fruit at the same level in all three treatments.
the contribution of potassium salts and hexoses to the total fruit osmotic pressure is different depending on the stage of fruit development.
the osmotic potential of fruit grown under saline conditions is not as high as expected, and that the contribution of potassium salts to fruit osmotic potential is greater than that of hexoses.
